sentences.t:
Hrōðgār maþelode — hē tō healle gēong,
stōd on stapole, geseah stēapne hrōf
golde fāhne ond Grendles hond —:
sentences.l: Hrothgar spoke in speech-words — he to the hall went, stood on the step, saw the steep roof gold-adorned and Grendel’s hand —:
sentences.i: Hrothgar spoke in formal words — he went to the hall, stood on the step, and saw the lofty roof, bright with gold, and Grendel’s hand —:
sentences.n: ‘maþelode’ is the house formula for a formal speech (‘spoke in speech-words’), and the dash and colon at the end tell us that the speech follows after what Hrothgar sees. The verbs ‘gēong’ (went), ‘stōd’ and ‘geseah’ (saw) are all past tense with ‘hē’ as subject. ‘stēapne hrōf golde fāhne’ is accusative: ‘fāhne’ agrees with ‘hrōf’ and means ‘variegated, adorned’ (the same word is ‘stained’ in 934), and ‘golde’ is a dative of means, ‘with gold’. ‘Grendles hond’ is a second object of ‘geseah’, joined to ‘hrōf’ by ‘ond’: the hand hangs from the roof where Beowulf’s victory left it. ‘stapole’ is the dative of ‘stapol’, ‘post, pillar, step’: ‘step’ is a guess at the exact spot, and ‘pillar’ is the other choice; some editors, as Klaeber’s apparatus shows, print ‘staþole’, which would be a different word, ‘foundation’, and the sense of where he stood is hardly changed.

sentences.t:
‘Ðisse ansȳne Alwealdan þanc
lungre gelimpe!
sentences.l: ‘For this sight to the All-ruler thanks swiftly happen!
sentences.i: ‘For this sight, let thanks go swiftly to the Ruler of all!
sentences.n: ‘gelimpe’ is a present subjunctive of ‘gelimpan’, ‘to happen, befall’, and the subjunctive makes a wish: ‘may thanks befall the All-ruler’. ‘Alwealdan’ is a dative (weak noun, ‘to the All-ruler’) and ‘þanc’ is the subject, so the wording is ‘thanks happen to him’ rather than ‘we give thanks’. ‘Ðisse ansȳne’ is a dative, ‘for this sight’, giving the reason. ‘Alwealdan’ is the same title for God that is ‘Alwalda’ at 955; the house rendering is ‘All-ruler’. ‘lungre’ is ‘quickly, soon’, an adverb.

sentences.t:
Fela ic lāþes gebād,
grynna æt Grendle;
sentences.l: Much I of harm endured, of afflictions at Grendel;
sentences.i: I have endured much that was hateful, many afflictions at Grendel’s hands;
sentences.n: ‘Fela’ (‘much, many’) takes a genitive, and ‘gebād’ (past of ‘gebīdan’, ‘to experience, live through’) can too, so ‘lāþes’ (genitive singular neuter, ‘of harm’, ‘lāð’ used as a noun for what is hateful) and ‘grynna’ (genitive plural of ‘gryn’) depend on one or both; the second stands beside the first and restates it. ‘grynna’ is taken from a word whose base sense is ‘snare, trap’, and ‘afflictions’ for the plural is a figurative reading that the lexica allow but do not fix, so call it a guess. ‘æt Grendle’ is ‘at (the hands of) Grendel’, with the dative of the name.

sentences.t:
ā mæg God wyrcan
wunder æfter wundre, wuldres Hyrde.
sentences.l: ever can God work wonder after wonder, keeper of glory.
sentences.i: God can always work wonder after wonder, the Keeper of glory.
sentences.n: ‘ā’ is ‘ever, always’, and ‘mæg’ is ‘can’, so the sentence states a rule about God, not one event. ‘wunder æfter wundre’ is ‘wonder after wonder’: ‘wunder’ is the object of ‘wyrcan’, and ‘wundre’ is the dative that ‘æfter’ takes. ‘wuldres Hyrde’ is in apposition to ‘God’: ‘Hyrde’ is ‘herdsman, keeper’ (the same word as in the epithet ‘fyrena hyrde’, ‘keeper of crimes’, in the house table) and ‘wuldres’ is the genitive of ‘wuldor’, ‘glory’. The title is thus ‘keeper of glory’; ‘herdsman’ is the older picture beneath it.

sentences.t:
Ðæt wæs ungeāra, þæt ic ǣnigra mē
wēana ne wēnde tō wīdan feore
bōte gebīdan, þonne blōde fāh
hūsa sēlest heorodrēorig stōd, —
sentences.l: That was not long since, that I of any woes for myself did not expect, for a wide life, remedy to live to see, when blood-stained, of houses best, sword-gory stood, —
sentences.i: It was not long ago that I never thought, for all my long life, to see a remedy for any of my woes — when the best of houses stood bloodstained, gory from the sword —
sentences.n: The main frame is ‘Ðæt wæs ungeāra, þæt ic … ne wēnde … bōte gebīdan’: ‘that was not long ago, that I did not expect to live to see relief’. ‘bōte’ is the object of ‘gebīdan’ (‘to live through, experience’), and ‘ǣnigra … wēana’ is a genitive plural depending on ‘bōte’: ‘relief for any woes’. ‘mē’ is a reflexive dative, ‘for myself’, and ‘tō wīdan feore’ is ‘for a wide life’, that is, for the rest of a long life. ‘ungeāra’ is ‘geāra’ (‘of old, long ago’) negated by ‘un-’, so ‘not long ago’ is a guess at the shade; the same word is ‘soon’ at 601 (Fitt IX), where the verb looks forward, and here ‘wæs’ looks back. ‘þonne’ here is ‘when’, and it introduces the picture of the hall in the past: ‘blōde fāh’ is ‘stained with blood’, ‘hūsa sēlest’ is ‘best of houses’ (genitive plural), and ‘heorodrēorig’ is ‘sword-gory’, from ‘heoru’, ‘sword’, and ‘drēorig’, ‘bloody’. The comma and dash at the end hand the sentence on to the next unit, which adds a clause about the woe of that time.

sentences.t:
wēa wīdscofen witena gehwylcum
ðāra þe ne wēndon, þæt hīe wīdeferhð
lēoda landgeweorc lāþum beweredon
scuccum ond scinnum.
sentences.l: woe widely thrust upon each of the counsellors of those who did not expect that they ever the people’s land-work against the hateful ones would defend, against demons and fiends.
sentences.i: Woe had been driven wide upon each of the counsellors, those who never expected to defend the people’s stronghold against its foes, against demons and spectres.
sentences.n: This is a loose unit: ‘wēa’ (‘woe’, nominative) with ‘wīdscofen’ (‘wide-shoved’, a past participle) has no verb, and the sense ‘woe was thrust far and wide’ is a guess from the pieces. Klaeber’s italic ‘um’ in ‘gehwylcum’ marks his change: the manuscript has ‘gehwylcne’ (accusative), and he reads the dative ‘to each’; editors who read ‘wēan wīdscufon’ make a plural verb instead, and the apparatus lists them. ‘witena gehwylcum ðāra þe ne wēndon’ is ‘to each of the counsellors, of those who did not expect’, and the clause that follows gives what they did not expect: ‘wīdeferhð’ is ‘ever, for all time’, ‘lēoda landgeweorc’ is ‘the people’s land-work’, that is, their fortified place, and ‘beweredon’ is a past subjunctive, ‘would defend’. ‘lāþum’ (‘the hateful ones’) with ‘scuccum’ (‘demons’) and ‘scinnum’ (‘fiends’) are datives of the enemy. ‘scinna’ is rare, and ‘spectres’ is a guess.

sentences.t:
Nū scealc hafað
þurh Drihtnes miht dǣd gefremede,
ðē wē ealle ǣr ne meahton
snyttrum besyrwan.
sentences.l: Now a retainer has through the Lord’s might a deed accomplished, which we all before could not by wits contrive.
sentences.i: Now a warrior has accomplished, through the Lord’s might, a deed that none of us, for all our wits, could contrive before.
sentences.n: ‘hafað … gefremede’ is the old perfect: ‘has’ plus a participle that agrees with the object, here ‘dǣd’ (a feminine accusative), so ‘has a deed done’. ‘scealc’ is ‘man, retainer’ and means Beowulf, unnamed. ‘þurh Drihtnes miht’ gives the source of the deed: ‘Drihten’ is ‘Lord’. ‘ðē’ is the relative ‘which’, with ‘dǣd’ as its antecedent, and ‘besyrwan’ (‘to plot, contrive, ensnare’) its verb, with ‘snyttrum’ (a dative plural, ‘by wits’) the means: no amount of cleverness had been able to bring the deed about.

sentences.t:
Hwæt, þæt secgan mæg
efne swā hwylc mægþa, swā ðone magan cende
æfter gumcynnum, gyf hēo gȳt lyfað,
þæt hyre Ealdmetod ēste wǣre
bearngebyrdo.
sentences.l: What! that may say even whichever of maidens, who that son bore among the races of men, if she yet lives, that to her the Old-Measurer was gracious in child-bearing.
sentences.i: Listen! Any woman among the races of men who bore this son, if she is still alive, may say that the ancient Lord was gracious to her in her child-bearing.
sentences.n: ‘Hwæt’ is ‘What!’ in the literal line and ‘Listen!’ in the idiomatic line, the house rendering. ‘secgan mæg’ is ‘may say’. The first ‘þæt’ is a pronoun pointing ahead (‘this’), and the second opens the clause that spells it out, ‘þæt … Ealdmetod ēste wǣre’: ‘that the Old-Measurer was gracious’, with the subjunctive ‘wǣre’ for what is said. ‘efne swā hwylc mægþa’ is ‘even whichever of the mægþ’: ‘mægþa’ is a genitive plural, and ‘mægþ’ means ‘maiden, woman’ (it is ‘maidens’ at 923) or else ‘kindred, tribe’; ‘woman’ fits ‘cende’ (‘bore’), so the literal line keeps ‘maidens’ and the idiomatic line says ‘woman’, but the word is uncertain. ‘swā ðone magan cende’ is ‘who bore that son’, ‘magan’ being ‘son, man’. ‘gyf hēo gȳt lyfað’ is ‘if she yet lives’. ‘Ealdmetod’ is ‘ancient Measurer’ (‘eald’, old, and ‘metod’, a name for God as the one who measures out fate); some editors print two words, as the apparatus says. ‘hyre’ is a dative, ‘to her’; ‘ēste’ is a predicate adjective, ‘gracious’; ‘bearngebyrdo’ is best taken as a dative of respect, ‘in child-bearing’, though its ending could also be a plural, so that is a guess. Hrothgar means that such a mother may say that God was gracious to her in bearing a son like Beowulf.

sentences.l: Now I, Beowulf, you, best of men, to myself as son will love in heart;
sentences.i: Now I, Beowulf, best of men, will love you in my heart as a son of my own;
sentences.n: ‘ic … wylle … þec … frēogan’ is ‘I will love you’; ‘frēogan’ is the infinitive, ‘to love, cherish’, and ‘mē for sunu’ is ‘for myself as a son’. ‘on ferhþe’ is ‘in the heart’. ‘secg[a] betsta’ is the address to Beowulf: ‘best of men’, with ‘secga’ a genitive plural. Klaeber puts the ‘a’ in brackets because the manuscript has ‘secg’ only, which would read ‘best man’; the added letter makes the usual ‘best of men’, and the apparatus lists one editor, with a query, who reads ‘secg [se]’ instead. Hrothgar’s words make Beowulf a son in affection.

sentences.t:
heald forð tela
nīwe sibbe.
sentences.l: hold henceforth well the new kinship.
sentences.i: Keep well, from now on, the new bond of kinship.
sentences.n: ‘heald’ is the imperative of ‘healdan’, ‘to hold, keep’, with ‘forð’ (‘henceforth’), ‘tela’ (‘well’), and the object ‘nīwe sibbe’, an accusative feminine ‘new kinship’. ‘sibb’ means ‘kinship’ and also ‘peace’; both senses are in play, and here the king means the kinship of a father and son.

sentences.t:
Ne bið þē [n]ǣnigra gād
worolde wilna, þē ic geweald hæbbe.
sentences.l: Not will be to you of any of the world’s wishes lack, of which I have power.
sentences.i: You shall lack nothing of the world’s wishes that I have power to give.
sentences.n: ‘Ne bið þē … gād’ is ‘there will not be to you a lack’; ‘gād’ is a neuter noun for ‘lack, want’ (the same phrase, ‘Ne bið þē … wilna gād’, is at 660 in Fitt IX), and ‘wilna’ is a genitive plural, ‘of wishes’, with ‘worolde’ (‘of the world’) before it: worldly wishes. ‘þē ic geweald hæbbe’ is ‘over which I have power’. Klaeber’s bracketed [n] and italic ‘a’ change the manuscript’s ‘ænigre’ (‘of any’, a feminine singular that does not match the plural ‘wilna’) into ‘nǣnigra’ (‘of none’), and the extra negative joins ‘Ne’ in the usual Old English piling-up of negatives, so ‘lack of no wishes’ means no lack at all. Other editors print ‘nǣnges’, as the apparatus says, and the sense is the same either way.

sentences.t:
Ful oft ic for lǣssan lēan teohhode,
hordweorþunge hnāhran rince,
sǣmran æt sæcce.
sentences.l: Full oft I for less reward appointed, hoard-honour to a lowlier man, a weaker one at the fight.
sentences.i: Very often I have fixed a reward, an honor of treasure, for a lesser deed, and given it to a humbler man, one weaker in the fight.
sentences.n: ‘for lǣssan’ is ‘for less’ (a lesser service), and ‘lēan teohhode’ is ‘ordained, appointed reward’ (‘teohhian’, ‘to appoint’; ‘lēan’, ‘reward’, the object). ‘hordweorþunge’ is the honor paid in treasure (‘hord’, ‘hoard’, and ‘weorþung’, ‘honoring’). ‘hnāhran rince’ and ‘sǣmran’ are datives and comparatives, ‘to a lowlier warrior, to a weaker one’; ‘hnāh’ is ‘low, mean’ and ‘sǣmra’ is ‘weaker, inferior’. ‘æt sæcce’ is ‘at the fight’. Hrothgar’s point is that Beowulf’s deed, which is greater than those, deserves a reward at least as great.

sentences.t:
Þū þē self hafast
dǣdum gefremed, þæt þīn [dōm] lyfað
āwa tō aldre.
sentences.l: You yourself have by deeds brought about that your [glory] lives ever to eternity.
sentences.i: You yourself have so acted that your glory will live for ever, for all time.
sentences.n: ‘Þū þē self’ is ‘you yourself’, ‘þē’ a reflexive dative. ‘hafast … gefremed’ is the perfect: ‘you have brought about’ with an uninflected participle and the clause ‘þæt … lyfað’ as its object, and ‘dǣdum’ (dative plural) is ‘by deeds’. ‘dōm’ is Klaeber’s bracketed addition, taken from Kemble; the manuscript has no noun, and ‘þīn lyfað’ (‘your lives’) needs one. Other editors suggest ‘mid dǣdum’ or a different ending on ‘gefremed’, as the apparatus says. ‘dōm’ is ‘judgment’ and so ‘reputation, glory’. ‘āwa tō aldre’ is ‘always, to the age’, that is, for ever.

sentences.t:
Alwalda þec
gōde forgylde, swā hē nū gȳt dyde!’
sentences.l: All-ruler you with good repay, as he now yet did!’
sentences.i: May the Ruler of all repay you with good, as He has done even now!’
sentences.n: ‘forgylde’ is a present subjunctive, a wish: ‘may he repay’, with ‘gōde’ (a dative, ‘with good’) the means. ‘Alwalda’ is ‘All-ruler’, the same title as ‘Alwealdan’ at 928. ‘swā hē nū gȳt dyde’ is ‘as he now yet did’: the past tense is looking back over what has just been done, so ‘as He has done even now’.

sentences.t: Bēowulf maþelode, bearn Ec[g]þēowes:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words, son of Ecgtheow:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words, son of Ecgtheow:
sentences.n: ‘maþelode’ and the colon are the house formula for a formal reply, the formula first used at 286, with the colon opening the speech. ‘bearn Ecgþēowes’ is ‘son of Ecgtheow’, in apposition to ‘Bēowulf’, with ‘Ecgþēowes’ a genitive. The manuscript has ‘Ec’ and Klaeber adds the ‘g’ in brackets (so too at 980), as the apparatus says. Ecgtheow is the father whose feud Hrothgar once settled, as Hrothgar told at 459–472.

sentences.t:
‘Wē þæt ellenweorc ēstum miclum,
feohtan fremedon, frēcne genēðdon
eafoð uncūþes.
sentences.l: ‘We that valor-work with great favor, the fight, performed, boldly dared the strength of the unknown.
sentences.i: ‘We carried out that deed of valor, the fight, with great goodwill, and boldly dared the might of one unknown.
sentences.n: ‘Wē … fremedon’ is ‘we performed’, with ‘þæt ellenweorc’ (‘that valor-work’, ‘that deed of valor’) as the object and ‘ēstum miclum’ (‘with great favor’, a dative of manner) as its adverb. ‘feohtan’ is either the noun ‘fight’ in apposition to the deed or the infinitive ‘to fight’; the sense is the same, and the parse is a guess. ‘frēcne’ is an adverb, ‘boldly’ (and also ‘dangerously’), and ‘genēðdon’ is ‘dared, ventured on’, taking an accusative, ‘eafoð’ (‘strength’). ‘uncūþes’ is a genitive, ‘of the unknown’, that is, of the unknown foe, Grendel.

sentences.t:
Ūþe ic swīþor,
þæt ðū hine selfne gesēon mōste,
fēond on frætewum fylwērigne!
sentences.l: I granted rather, that you him himself might see, the fiend in his trappings, fall-weary!
sentences.i: I would rather that you could have seen him himself, the fiend in his trappings, wearied unto death!
sentences.n: ‘Ūþe ic swīþor’ is ‘I granted more’, the past of ‘unnan’ (‘to grant, wish’, as at 501 in Fitt VIII) with the adverb ‘swīþor’ (‘more, rather’), so ‘I would rather’; the clause ‘þæt … mōste’ with the subjunctive says what he wishes. ‘gesēon mōste’ is ‘might see’, and ‘hine selfne’ is ‘him himself’, an accusative: Beowulf would have wished Hrothgar to see the whole body, not only a hand. ‘on frætewum’ is ‘in his trappings’ (‘frætwe’ are ornaments, gear); the word is odd for a monster, so ‘in his trappings’ is a loose reading and a guess. ‘fylwērigne’ is an accusative adjective, ‘weary to the fall’ (‘fyll’, ‘fall’), so ‘wearied unto death’.

sentences.t:
Ic hine hrædlīce heardan clammum
on wælbedde wrīþan þōhte,
þæt hē for mundgripe mīnum scolde
licgean līfbysig, būtan his līc swice;
sentences.l: I him quickly with hard clasps on the slaughter-bed to bind thought, that he for my hand-grip should lie life-busy, unless his body should fail;
sentences.i: I meant to bind him swiftly in hard clasps on his slaughter-bed, so that he should lie before my hand-grip, struggling for his life, unless his body gave out;
sentences.n: ‘Ic … þōhte … wrīþan’ is ‘I thought to bind’; ‘hine’ is its object, with ‘heardan clammum’ (‘with hard clasps’) as means. Klaeber’s italic ‘ne’ marks his change: the manuscript has ‘him’, and ‘hine’ is Thorkelin’s reading. ‘on wælbedde’ is ‘on the slaughter-bed’, the bed where he would die. The italic ‘mu’ in ‘mundgripe’ marks another change: the manuscript has ‘handgripe’ (‘hand-grip’), and ‘mund’ (also ‘hand’) is Kemble’s change, so the sense is the same. ‘for mundgripe mīnum’ is ‘before my hand-grip’, with ‘for’ and the dative. ‘licgean līfbysig’ is ‘lie life-busy’, busy for his life, that is, struggling. ‘būtan his līc swice’ is a subjunctive, ‘unless his body fail’ (‘swīcan’, ‘fail, give way’), that is, until he died.

sentences.t:
ic hine ne mihte, þā Metod nolde,
ganges getwǣman, nō ic him þæs georne ætfealh,
feorhgenīðlan; wæs tō foremihtig
fēond on fēþe.
sentences.l: I him not could, when the Measurer would not, from going cut off, not I to him for that eagerly clung, the life-foe; was too over-mighty the fiend in going.
sentences.i: I could not, since God would not have it, cut him off from going, nor did I cling to him closely enough, my deadly foe; the fiend was too mighty in his going.
sentences.n: ‘ic hine ne mihte … ganges getwǣman’ is ‘I could not cut him off from his going’; ‘getwǣman’ takes a genitive of the thing, ‘ganges’. ‘þā Metod nolde’ is ‘when the Measurer would not’, with ‘þā’ as ‘when, since’, and ‘Metod’ is ‘Measurer’, an old name of God (the house rendering). ‘nō ic him þæs georne ætfealh’ is ‘I did not cling to him closely enough’: ‘ætfealh’ is the past of ‘ætfeolan’, ‘to stick, cling’, and ‘þæs’ with ‘georne’ means ‘so eagerly’. ‘feorhgenīðlan’ is an accusative, ‘life-enemy’, in apposition to ‘hine’. ‘foremihtig’ is ‘very mighty’, and ‘tō’ before it adds ‘too’. ‘on fēþe’ is ‘in going’: ‘fēþe’ is ‘going, travel on foot’, so the fiend was too strong to be held when he made off; the exact sense is a guess.

sentences.l: Yet he his hand left, for life-protection, the track to guard, arm and shoulder;
sentences.i: Yet he left his hand behind, to save his life, to keep the trail — arm and shoulder;
sentences.n: ‘Hwæþere’ is ‘yet’. ‘hē his folme forlēt’ is ‘he left his hand’; ‘tō līfwraþe’ is ‘for life-protection’, a compound whose sense I read from its parts, so a guess. ‘lāst weardian’ is ‘to guard the track’, an infinitive of purpose: the plainest reading is that the hand stays behind as the trace of his flight. This too is a guess. ‘earm ond eaxle’ is ‘arm and shoulder’, an accusative apposition to ‘folme’ telling how much he left.

sentences.t:
nō þǣr ǣnịge swā þēah
fēasceaft guma frōfre gebohte;
sentences.l: not there any, however, wretched man comfort bought;
sentences.i: Yet the wretched creature gained no comfort by it;
sentences.n: ‘nō … ǣnịge … frōfre gebohte’ is ‘not … any comfort bought’: ‘ǣnịge’ is an accusative feminine agreeing with ‘frōfre’ (‘comfort’), and ‘gebohte’ is the past of ‘gebycgan’, ‘to buy, obtain’. ‘þǣr’ is ‘there’, that is, in that matter, ‘swā þēah’ is ‘even so’. ‘fēasceaft’ is ‘wretched’ (literally ‘few-made’, poor in everything), ‘guma’ is ‘man’, and the sentence says that the loss of the hand bought him no relief. The dot under the the idiomatic line in ‘ǣnịge’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre.

sentences.t:
nō þȳ leng leofað lāðgetēona
synnum geswenced, ac hyne sār hafað
in nīdgripe nearwe befongen,
balwon bendum;
sentences.l: none the longer lives the hateful-injurer, by sins afflicted, but him pain has in a violent grip narrowly enclosed, with baleful bonds;
sentences.i: He lives none the longer for it, that hateful ravager, burdened with his sins; but pain holds him tightly enclosed in a violent grip, in baleful bonds;
sentences.n: ‘nō þȳ leng leofað’ is ‘none the longer lives’, ‘þȳ’ an instrumental, ‘by that’. ‘lāðgetēona’ is a compound of ‘lāð’ (‘hateful’) and ‘getēona’ (‘injurer’), a hateful harmer, and ‘synnum’ means ‘by sins’, here crimes. ‘hyne sār hafað … befongen’ is ‘pain has him enclosed’: ‘sār’ is the subject, ‘hyne’ the object and ‘befongen’ the participle. Klaeber’s italic ‘n’ in ‘nīdgripe’ is his change: the manuscript has ‘mid gripe’, ‘with a grip’, and he reads ‘nīd’ (‘force’), so ‘violent grip’; others read ‘nȳd-’ (‘need, compulsion’) or ‘nīð-’ (‘hostility’), and the apparatus lists them. ‘balwon bendum’ is a dative plural, ‘with baleful bonds’, and ‘nearwe’ is ‘tightly’.

sentences.t:
ðǣr ābīdan sceal
maga māne fāh miclan dōmes,
hū him scīr Metod scrīfan wille.’
sentences.l: there to await must the kinsman with crime stained the great judgment, how to him the bright Measurer will decree.’
sentences.i: There the man stained with crime must await the great judgment, and how the bright Lord will decree for him.’
sentences.n: ‘ðǣr’ is ‘there’, the place of the judgment, and ‘ābīdan sceal’ is ‘must await’, taking a genitive, ‘miclan dōmes’ (‘the great doom’). ‘maga’ is ‘man, kinsman’ and ‘māne fāh’ is ‘stained with crime’ (‘mān’, ‘crime’, a dative). ‘hū him scīr Metod scrīfan wille’ is an indirect question: ‘how the bright Measurer will decree for him’, with ‘scrīfan’ (‘to assign, decree’, the word behind ‘shrive’) taking a dative. ‘scīr’ is ‘bright’, and Metod is the house ‘Measurer’ in the literal line, with ‘Lord’ in the idiomatic line. The closing quote after ‘wille’ ends Beowulf’s speech.

sentences.t:
Ðā wæs swīgra secg, sunu Ec[g]lāfes,
on gylpsprǣce gūðgeweorca,
siþðan æþelingas eorles cræfte
ofer hēanne hrōf hand scēawedon,
fēondes fingras;
sentences.l: Then was more silent the man, Ecglaf’s son, in boasting-speech of war-works, after the athelings by the earl’s craft over the high roof the hand looked at, the fiend’s fingers;
sentences.i: Then Ecglaf’s son was more silent in his boasting of warlike deeds, after the princes, thanks to the earl’s craft, had looked at the hand above them, under the high roof, the fiend’s fingers;
sentences.n: ‘Ðā wæs swīgra secg’ is ‘then was more silent the man’, with ‘swīgra’ the comparative of ‘swīge’, ‘silent’; ‘sunu Ecglāfes’ is Unferth, the Dane who challenged Beowulf at 499. The manuscript has ‘Ec’ for ‘Ecg-’, and Klaeber adds the ‘g’ in brackets, as the apparatus says. ‘on gylpsprǣce gūðgeweorca’ is ‘in boast-speech of war-works’: ‘gūðgeweorca’ is a genitive plural saying what he had boasted about. ‘siþðan … scēawedon’ is ‘after they looked at’, with ‘hand’ as object, ‘fēondes fingras’ in apposition, and ‘eorles cræfte’ (a dative of means) is Beowulf’s skill. ‘ofer hēanne hrōf’ is ‘over the high roof’; the hand hangs from the roof, so ‘above them, under the roof’ is a loose reading of ‘ofer’.

sentences.t:
foran ǣghwylc wæs,
stīð[r]a nægla gehwylc stȳle gelīcost,
hǣþẹnes handsporu hilderinces
egl[u] unhēoru;
sentences.l: in front each was, of the stiff nails each most like steel, the heathen’s hand-spurs, the warrior’s, [hateful] monstrous;
sentences.i: Each nail at the front was most like steel — the heathen warrior’s hand-spurs, hateful and monstrous;
sentences.n: This unit is the hardest in the part. ‘foran ǣghwylc wæs’ is ‘in front each was’, the nails at the tips; ‘stīð[r]a nægla gehwylc’ is ‘each of the stiff nails’, ‘stȳle gelīcost’ is ‘most like steel’ (a dative of comparison). Klaeber’s italic ‘ī’ and bracketed [r] change the manuscript’s ‘steda’ to ‘stīðra’, a genitive plural; the apparatus lists others, and several editors want ‘gehwylc’ cancelled. ‘hǣþẹnes handsporu hilderinces’ is ‘the heathen warrior’s hand-spurs’, that is, claws; ‘handsporu’ occurs only here, and some editors change it to ‘-speru’ (‘hand-spears’). The dot under the ‘ẹ’ in ‘hǣþẹnes’ is the same metre sign as at 972. ‘egl[u] unhēoru’ are adjectives for ‘handsporu’, ‘hateful, monstrous’. The manuscript has ‘egl’, and Klaeber’s [u] makes it a plural adjective, where Kemble made it a noun ‘egle’. ‘unhēoru’ (‘un-’ plus ‘hēoru’, ‘gentle’) is ‘monstrous’, a guess.

sentences.t:
ǣghwylc gecwæð,
þæt him heardra nān hrīnan wolde
īren ǣrgōd, þæt ðæs āhlǣcan
blōdge beadufolme onberan wolde.
sentences.l: each said that to him of hard ones none, iron good of old, would touch, that on the awesome one’s bloody battle-hand would bear.
sentences.i: Each said that no iron, however hard and tried of old, would touch it, nor make a mark on the fearsome one’s bloody battle-hand.
sentences.n: ‘ǣghwylc gecwæð’ is ‘each said’, now of the men, not the nails (the same word was the nails’ at 984). The speech has two clauses, both with ‘wolde’, ‘would’: ‘þæt him … hrīnan wolde’, ‘that would touch it’ (‘hrīnan’ takes a dative; ‘him’ is the fiend or his hand), and ‘þæt … onberan wolde’. ‘heardra nān īren ǣrgōd’ is ‘none of the hard ones, iron good from of old’, with ‘heardra’ a genitive plural and ‘ǣrgōd’ ‘good from of old’ (‘ǣr-’, ‘before’, as in the epithet for Hrothgar at 130). ‘ðæs āhlǣcan’ (‘of the awesome one’, a genitive) and ‘blōdge beadufolme’ (‘the bloody battle-hand’, a dative) go with ‘onberan’ (‘to bear on, bring to bear on’, taking a dative), whose exact sense, ‘make a mark on’, is a guess. Some editors change the second ‘þæt’ to ‘þē’ (‘who’) and refer it to Beowulf, as the apparatus says.
